      Warm-up

      Pinhole camera warm-up

      1 entries

      Question Warm-upTextbook p. 200

      Answer

      The screen shows a real, inverted image of the bulb. Rays travel in straight lines through the small hole. Rays from the top reach the lower screen and rays from the bottom reach the upper screen. Its size relative to the bulb depends on the two distances.

      Quick check

      Plane-mirror images

      3 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 205

      Answer

      The minimum mirror height is 1.0 m, half of 2 m. The extreme reflection points are halfway in height between the eye and the top of the head, and between the eye and the feet. The mirror must be mounted at the correct height.

      Question 2Textbook p. 205

      Answer

      The glass reflects some indoor light all day. At night the view through the window is dark, so the reflection stands out. Daytime light transmitted from outdoors can swamp the faint indoor reflection.

      Question 3Textbook p. 205

      Answer

      1. Extend reflected rays backward to locate a virtual image.
      2. It is behind the mirror as far as you are in front.
      3. The image moves closer to the mirror by the same distance. Your separation from the image decreases twice as fast.
      Investigation

      Investigation 7-1A · Image location

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 206

      Answer

      The unlit candle lines up with a virtual image behind the sheet. The image is as far behind the reflecting surface as the lit candle is in front. Check alignment from more than one viewing position to reduce parallax.

      Question 2Textbook p. 206

      Answer

      Reflection occurs at the air–plastic interfaces. The front surface usually gives the brighter reflection. Light transmitted into the sheet can reflect at the back surface and emerge to give a faint offset image.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-1A · Reflected rays

      3 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 207

      Answer

      Measure perpendicular to the reflecting surface. The ideal result is equal distance magnitudes. Finite beam width, an inaccurate mirror line, and measurement errors can shift the measured intersection.

      Question 2Textbook p. 207

      Answer

      Reflected rays diverge in front of the mirror. Extending them backward makes them appear to meet behind it. The light actually originates at the bulb filament in front.

      Question 3Textbook p. 207

      Answer

      Each incident angle equals its reflected angle, measured from the normal. This is the same law used for wavefronts reflecting from a plane barrier. Report your observed differences and angle uncertainty.

      Challenge

      Investigation 7-1A · Photographing a mirror image

      1 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 207

      Answer

      Set the focus to about 4 m if the camera is also 2 m from the mirror and next to your face. The virtual image is 2 m behind the mirror. In general add the appropriate object and camera distances for a head-on setup.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-1B · Multiple images

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 209

      Answer

      For the usual symmetric setup and when 360°/θ is an integer, the textbook model gives N = 360°/θ − 1. At 90° this gives 3 images. Finite mirrors can hide some images. For an odd integer ratio, moving the object off the bisector can change the count. Parallel facing mirrors can give a long chain of reflections.

      Question 2Textbook p. 209

      Answer

      Four copies include the object, so 360°/θ = 4. The angle is 90°.

      Challenge

      Investigation 7-1B · Infinity box and periscope

      2 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 209

      Answer

      With the object centred, opposing mirror walls reflect each other repeatedly. Each successive image is normally dimmer. The floor mirror also gives images below the apparent floor.

      Question 2Textbook p. 209

      Answer

      Put two plane mirrors at 45° to the tube, with their reflective faces parallel and oriented to send the light down the tube and then toward the eye. Two reflections preserve the scene’s orientation.

      Section review

      7.1 Review · Reflection and the spectrum

      13 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      For electromagnetic radiation in vacuum, c = fλ. All bands have the same c, so higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.

      Question 2Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      The visible spectrum is the range detectable by the human eye, about 380–760 nm using the textbook’s limits. Violet is at the short-wavelength end and red at the long-wavelength end.

      Question 3Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      Infrared lies beyond red and is emitted by warm objects. Radio waves have longer wavelengths still and are used in broadcasting. Microwaves are another example.

      Question 4Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      Infrared, microwaves, and radio waves all have lower frequencies than visible light.

      Question 5Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      The incident and reflected angles are equal when measured from the normal at the point of reflection. The rays and normal lie in the same plane. A bathroom mirror is a familiar example.

      Question 6Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      Place a mirror near the corner so the incident ray from the hidden object reflects toward your eye. Draw the normal perpendicular to the mirror where the ray hits. Rotate the mirror until the reflected and incident rays make equal angles with that normal.

      Question 7Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      Object distance is measured from the object to the mirror. Image distance is measured from the mirror to the image. Their magnitudes match for a plane mirror. The image distance is negative in the signed convention because that image is virtual.

      Question 8Textbook p. 210

      Answer

      No light converges at the apparent image behind the plane mirror. The rays reaching your eye only appear to originate there. You cannot catch the virtual image on a screen behind the mirror.

      Question 9Textbook p. 211

      Answer

      1. 5 at 60°.
      2. 7 at 45°.
      3. 23 at 15°.
      4. 35 at 10°.
      5. 359 at 1° in the ideal model.

      Use 360°/θ − 1 for these symmetric arrangements. Physical size and the field of view limit what you can actually see.

      Question 10Textbook p. 211

      Answer

      The shortest mirror is 90 cm high. The two points of reflection lie halfway in height between the eye and the head and between the eye and the feet. Their vertical separation is half the person’s height regardless of distance from the mirror.

      Question 11Textbook p. 211

      Answer

      Mirrored lettering on the ambulance reads normally in the driver’s rear-view mirror. To mirror your name, reverse the letter order and flip each letter across a vertical line. Draw the upright stroke of a b to the left of its loop, then place the stroke at the same distance on the right of the loop in the reflected view to obtain d.

      Question 12Textbook p. 211

      Answer

      A ray from the top passes through the hole and reaches the lower screen. The image is real and inverted. Its size ratio is screen distance from the hole divided by object distance from the hole.

      Question 13Textbook p. 211

      Answer

      Use two right-angle prisms whose hypotenuse faces are parallel. Light enters the first prism perpendicular to a leg, reflects internally at 45°, and exits down the tube. The second prism turns it toward the eye.

      Warm-up

      Spoon mirrors warm-up

      1 entries

      Question Warm-upTextbook p. 212

      Answer

      The concave bowl can give an inverted image from farther away and an upright, enlarged one when your face is inside its focal length. The convex back gives an upright, reduced virtual image. A spoon’s non-spherical shape can distort the image.

      Concave mirror ray diagrams

      1 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 215

      Answer

      In order, the drawings place the object beyond C, at C, and between C and F. From the arrow tip, draw a ray parallel to the axis and reflect it through F. A second ray through the vertex reflects at equal angles to the axis. Their intersections give the image tips.

      Object positionImage
      dₒ > 2fReal, inverted, reduced. Between f and 2f in front of the mirror.

      Sample prompt

      Sample 7.2.1 · Using the mirror equation

      1 entries

      Question 7.2.1Textbook p. 217

      Answer

      Convert 1.00 m to 100 cm. 1/dᵢ = 1/20.0 − 1/100 = 0.0400 cm⁻¹, so dᵢ = +25.0 cm. The image is real and forms in front of the mirror.

      Practice

      Practice 7.2.1 · Using the mirror equation

      4 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 218

      Answer

      Real image gives dᵢ = +25.0 cm. 1/dₒ = 1/20.0 − 1/25.0 = 0.0100 cm⁻¹. The object is 100 cm in front.

      Question 2Textbook p. 218

      Answer

      With dᵢ = dₒ, 2/dₒ = 1/f. Thus dₒ = dᵢ = 2f. The object is at C for a spherical concave mirror in the paraxial model.

      Question 3Textbook p. 218

      Answer

      1/f = 1/20.0 + 1/40.0 = 0.0750 cm⁻¹. The focal length is 13.3 cm.

      Question 4Textbook p. 218

      Answer

      1/dᵢ = 1/15.0 − 1/10.0 = −1/30.0 cm⁻¹. dᵢ = −30.0 cm indicates an upright virtual image 30.0 cm behind the mirror.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-2A · Convex mirrors

      4 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 220

      Answer

      Parallel incoming rays spread apart after reflection. Their backward extensions meet near a virtual focus behind the convex mirror.

      Question 2Textbook p. 220

      Answer

      The curved surface presents different local normals across its width. It can direct rays from a wider range of directions to the eye, at the cost of reduced image size.

      Question 3Textbook p. 220

      Answer

      For a real object, a convex mirror gives a virtual, upright, reduced image behind the mirror, between the vertex and F.

      Question 4Textbook p. 220

      Answer

      A vertical cylindrical mirror curves across its width and is straight vertically. With a convex side facing you, your image looks narrower while the vertical scale is much less changed. A concave side close enough can stretch the width instead.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-2A · Concave mirrors

      3 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 221

      Answer

      Rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflecting. In the paraxial approximation the crossing is at the principal focus.

      Question 2Textbook p. 221

      Answer

      A concave primary mirror collects light from a distant object and forms a real image near the focus. A larger mirror intercepts more light. An eyepiece or sensor views that image.

      Question 3Textbook p. 221

      Answer

      A cylindrical mirror curves in only one direction, so it can focus a parallel sheet of rays to a line. The ray-box view shows a cross-section. Rays far from the axis can also show aberration.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-2A · Measuring focal length

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 221

      Answer

      If 1.5 m exceeds f, the rays still converge to a real image. Use 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/(1.5 m), so dᵢ > f for a finite distance. If dₒ = f they leave parallel, and if dₒ < f the image is virtual.

      Question 2Textbook p. 221

      Answer

      A distant source supplies nearly parallel rays. With 1/dₒ ≈ 0, the mirror equation reduces to dᵢ ≈ f. Locate the sharpest image on a screen and measure from the mirror vertex.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-2B · Images in concave mirrors

      6 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      The first three placements yield real images. At f the reflected rays from an object point are parallel, so there is no real image at a finite distance.

      Object positionImage
      dₒ > 2fReal, inverted, reduced. Between f and 2f in front of the mirror.
      dₒ = 2fReal, inverted, same size. At 2f in front of the mirror.
      f < dₒ < 2fReal, inverted, enlarged. Beyond 2f in front of the mirror.
      dₒ = fOutgoing rays from each object point are parallel. No finite image.
      Question 2Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      A distant star gives nearly parallel incident rays. Its real image forms near the focal plane, about f in front of the mirror.

      Question 3Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      Put the filament at the principal focus to obtain a nearly parallel outgoing beam. A source of finite size gives some beam spread.

      Question 4Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      At dₒ = f, 1/dᵢ = 0. Rays from each object point leave parallel, so there is no finite screen position that gives a sharp image.

      Question 5Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      A real object must be farther than the focus, so dₒ > f. The reflected rays then cross in front of the mirror.

      Question 6Textbook p. 222

      Answer

      For 0 < dₒ < f the reflected rays diverge. They appear to originate from an upright virtual image behind the mirror.

      Section review

      7.2 Review · Curved mirrors

      10 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      A simple convex lens is thicker at the centre than at its edges. A simple concave lens is thinner at the centre. In air with ordinary glass, the first converges parallel rays and the second diverges them.

      Question 2Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      A converging lens brings an axial parallel bundle to a real focus. A diverging lens makes it spread as if from a virtual focus on the incoming side.

      Question 3Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      A convex mirror always reduces a real object. A concave mirror can also reduce an object placed beyond C, giving a real inverted image in that case.

      Question 4Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      1. Concave, with your face inside f for a magnified upright image.
      2. Convex for a wide field of view.
      3. Plane for an upright, undistorted, same-size view.
      Question 5Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      In order, E, A, F, B, D, C. The vertex is where the principal axis meets the surface. For a spherical mirror in the small-angle approximation, |f| = R/2.

      Question 6Textbook p. 223

      Answer

      Object positionImage
      Far awayNear F, real, inverted, strongly reduced
      Beyond CBetween F and C, real, inverted, reduced
      At CAt C, real, inverted, same size
      Between F and CBeyond C, real, inverted, enlarged
      At FNo finite image
      Between F and vertexBehind mirror, virtual, upright, enlarged
      Question 7Textbook p. 224

      Answer

      Object positionImage
      dₒ > 2fReal, inverted, reduced. Between f and 2f in front of the mirror.
      f < dₒ < 2fReal, inverted, enlarged. Beyond 2f in front of the mirror.
      dₒ = fOutgoing rays from each object point are parallel. No finite image.
      0 < dₒ < fVirtual, upright, enlarged. Behind the mirror.
      Question 8Textbook p. 224

      Answer

      1. Make it concave across the width and stand inside f to appear wider.
      2. Make it convex across the width to appear narrower.
      3. Make it convex in the vertical cross-section to compress height.
      4. Make it concave in the vertical cross-section and stand inside f to stretch height.
      Question 9Textbook p. 224

      Answer

      Draw one incoming ray parallel to the axis. Reflect it so its backward extension passes through F. A second ray striking the vertex reflects at the same angle to the axis. Extend the reflected rays behind the mirror. They meet at a reduced, upright image between F and the vertex.

      Question 10Textbook p. 225

      Answer

      1. For the real object shown in the usual classroom setup, no. Reflected rays diverge and only their extensions meet.
      2. No for a real object. With f < 0 and dₒ > 0, |dᵢ| = |f|dₒ/(|f| + dₒ) < dₒ, so |m| < 1.
      Challenge

      Curved mirrors challenge · The Mirage

      1 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 225

      Answer

      The image is real. Light from the object at the bottom reflects from the upper concave surface and then from the lower one. The rays really meet near the opening. The mirrors are positioned so the first reflection supplies a bundle the second can focus there.

      Warm-up

      Pencil in water warm-up

      1 entries

      Question Warm-upTextbook p. 226

      Answer

      The part under water appears displaced, so the pencil seems bent at the surface. Rays from the submerged part speed up and bend away from the normal as they enter air. Your eye traces them back along straight lines to a shallower virtual position.

      Quick check

      Snell’s law and dispersion

      4 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 228

      Answer

      Use n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n(air) ≈ 1.00. n(glass) = sin 18.5°/sin 12.0° ≈ 1.53.

      Question 2Textbook p. 228

      Answer

      With n(diamond) = 2.42, θ₂ = sin⁻¹(sin 10.0°/2.42) ≈ 4.11° from the normal.

      Question 3Textbook p. 228

      Answer

      1. It slows and bends toward the normal. θ(glass) = sin⁻¹(sin 30°/1.500) ≈ 19.5°.
      2. It speeds up and bends away from the normal. Snell’s law gives an exit angle of 30°. For parallel faces and air on both sides, the exiting ray is parallel to the incoming ray and shifted sideways.
      Question 4Textbook p. 228

      Answer

      A prism disperses white light because the refractive index depends on wavelength. In ordinary glass, violet is refracted more than red.

      Quick check

      Critical angles

      3 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 230

      Answer

      Assume a diamond–air interface. sin θc = 1.00/2.42, so θc = 24.4°.

      Question 2Textbook p. 230

      Answer

      For glass to air, θc = sin⁻¹(1.000/1.500) = 41.8°.

      Question 3Textbook p. 230

      Answer

      For the material to air, n = 1.00/sin 52.0° = 1.27. The index depends on the surrounding medium if it is other than air.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-3A · Refraction in water

      3 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 233

      Answer

      Light slows down in water or Plexiglas. At oblique incidence it bends toward the normal and its wavelength decreases. Its frequency remains fixed. At normal incidence it continues straight.

      Question 2Textbook p. 233

      Answer

      With θᵢ vertical and θᵣ horizontal as instructed, the small-angle slope Δθᵢ/Δθᵣ is dimensionless and approximately n(material)/n(air). Use measured points near the origin. Plexiglas usually gives a larger slope and a greater bend than water. Plot sin θᵢ vertically against sin θᵣ horizontally for a straight-line fit over all angles. Its slope is n(material)/n(air).

      Question 3Textbook p. 233

      Answer

      Yes. Both light and water waves can change speed at a boundary while their frequency stays fixed. Both bend toward the normal when going into a slower region at oblique incidence.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-3B · Internal reflection and critical angle

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 234

      Answer

      Compare your observed last grazing refracted ray with θc = sin⁻¹[n(air)/n(material)]. Typical predictions are 48.8° for water (n ≈ 1.33) and 42.2° for acrylic (n ≈ 1.49). If the sample is glass, use its measured index. For n = 1.50, θc = 41.8°.

      Question 2Textbook p. 234

      Answer

      Draw successive reflections at the inside wall of the pipe. At each wall, construct the local normal and use equal incident and reflected angles. Total internal reflection continues wherever the incidence angle exceeds the plastic–air critical angle. A very sharp bend can let light escape.

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-3C · Polarization

      4 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 236

      Answer

      A polarizer selects a transverse electric-field direction, and a second crossed polarizer can block that component. This directional behaviour is evidence of the transverse wave nature of light. Photons also carry polarization in the quantum description.

      Question 2Textbook p. 236

      Answer

      Light reflected from a horizontal road or water surface is often strongly horizontally polarized. A vertical transmission axis suppresses much of that glare.

      Question 3Textbook p. 236

      Answer

      Rotate the filter to reduce the reflected glare. This can increase contrast and make detail below the surface easier to see. The effect depends on viewing angle.

      Question 4Textbook p. 236

      Answer

      Calcite separates an incident beam into two rays with different polarizations by birefringence. An ordinary calcite crystal can transmit both, so the crystal alone differs from a filter that absorbs one component. A device can isolate one of the two rays.

      Section review

      7.3 Review · Refraction of light

      13 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      The shown ray is 20° to the water surface, hence 70° to the normal. This exceeds the water–air critical angle of about 49°, so the ray is totally internally reflected. Other rays from the fish can leave the water at smaller incidence angles and reach the fisher.

      Question 2Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      1. Choice iii. Aim below the apparent position, toward the real fish. Rays from the fish bend away from the normal as they leave water, making it appear shallower.
      2. Aim the laser along the line of sight toward the apparent position. Refraction is reversible, so the beam will bend toward the normal on entering water and follow the sight ray back to the real fish.
      Question 3Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      Some rays reflect directly at the front air–glass surface. Others enter the glass, reflect off the rear coating, and refract out. For a thick sheet and an oblique view, the two reflected bundles are offset. Further internal bounces can give still fainter images.

      Question 4Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      For glass to air, θc = sin⁻¹(1/1.58) ≈ 39.3°.

      Question 5Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      λ = c/f = (3.00 × 10⁸)/(5.00 × 10¹⁴) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm.

      Question 6Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      v = c/n = (3.00 × 10⁸)/2.42 = 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s.

      Question 7Textbook p. 237

      Answer

      Matching phase along the boundary gives sin θ₁/λ₁ = sin θ₂/λ₂. Since λ = v/f, f is unchanged, and v = c/n, this becomes n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. The angles are measured from the normal.

      Question 8Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      1.33 is an approximate value for visible light in ordinary water. Index depends on wavelength and on water conditions such as temperature and composition. It is defined relative to the vacuum speed c.

      Question 9Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      1. The three processes are refraction, dispersion, and internal reflection.
      2. Look toward rain or spray with the Sun behind you. A primary rainbow is centred on the direction opposite the Sun.
      3. From the outside or top to the inside of a primary bow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. The colours form a continuum.
      Question 10Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      In a vacuum, red, green, and blue all travel at c. In ordinary glass with normal dispersion, red has the lowest index of the three and travels fastest.

      Question 11Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      v = c/n ≈ (3.0 × 10⁸)/1.50 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

      Question 12Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      n = c/v = (3.00 × 10⁸)/(1.95 × 10⁸) ≈ 1.54 for the given quartz ray.

      Question 13Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      1. The frequency stays fixed, so λ(water) = λ(air)/n ≈ 650/1.33 = 489 nm.
      2. Light with 489 nm wavelength in air would appear blue-green.
      3. The transmitted light has the same frequency as the 650 nm red light in air. Colour perception follows that frequency, so it still looks red.
      Challenge

      Refraction Brain Stretch

      7 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      Diamond’s high refractive index gives a small critical angle. Properly cut facets send light through repeated internal reflections and back toward the viewer. Dispersion separates wavelengths into coloured flashes.

      Question 2Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      The signal is encoded as light pulses. The higher-index core guides light within the lower-index cladding. A detector converts the pulses back into an electrical signal.

      Question 3Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      Near the horizon, light bends through layers of changing air density. The Sun appears higher than its geometric position, so it is visible a little before geometric sunrise and a little after geometric sunset.

      Question 4Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      A strong temperature gradient changes the refractive index with height and curves light rays. Above hot pavement, rays from the sky can bend upward toward the eye and appear to come from the ground, making a water-like image.

      Question 5Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      Rays from the bottom bend away from the normal as they leave water. Their straight backward extensions meet at a shallower apparent depth. Viewed close to straight down, apparent depth ≈ actual depth/n(water).

      Question 6Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      A gem tester can compare thermal conductivity, which is much higher for diamond than for ordinary glass. A specialist can corroborate with optical tests or microscopy. Sparkle by itself is an unreliable identifier.

      Question 7Textbook p. 238

      Answer

      One optical effect is that curved, thick glass walls can change the apparent shape or width of the liquid column. Measure the actual volume to test whether apparent size matches capacity. The glass design can also reflect strength or insulation considerations.

      Warm-up

      Looking through lenses warm-up

      1 entries

      Question Warm-upTextbook p. 239

      Answer

      A converging lens close to the text can give an upright, enlarged virtual image when the text is inside f. A diverging lens gives an upright, reduced virtual image. A converging lens held farther away can instead form a real, inverted image. Describe the lens and distance you actually used.

      Quick check

      Tracing rays through lenses

      2 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 242

      Answer

      A ray parallel to the axis leaves through F₂. A ray through F₁ leaves parallel, and a ray through the centre continues straight. The object position determines the image. For example, if dₒ > 2f, the rays cross on the far side between f and 2f, giving a real, inverted, reduced image. The three ray rules alone do not specify a unique object distance.

      Object positionImage
      dₒ > 2fReal, inverted, reduced. Between f and 2f on the opposite side of the lens.
      Question 2Textbook p. 242

      Answer

      For a real object, rays leaving a diverging lens spread. Backward extensions meet on the object side, between the lens and near focus. The image is virtual, upright, and reduced.

      Quick check

      The thin-lens equation

      3 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 244

      Answer

      Investigation

      Investigation 7-4A · Focusing with lenses

      4 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 249

      Answer

      Start with the unaided view in the empty tube. With a nearly flat water surface, the coin appears closer and subtends a larger angle from the same eye position. A convex water surface adds converging power and can magnify the coin when it is inside the effective focus. Compare your circles with the same eye position.

      Question 2Textbook p. 249

      Answer

      A concave cylindrical lens makes the ray sheet spread. A convex one brings it together in the cross-section. In contact, their powers add, so similar opposite powers nearly cancel. Separating the lenses changes how wide and how convergent the bundle is at the second lens.

      Question 3Textbook p. 249

      Answer

      1. Hold the text closer than the water-filled flask’s focal length. It acts like a converging lens and gives a magnified upright virtual image.
      2. Place the flame farther away than f. Move the flask or screen until the real, inverted image is sharp on the wall.
      Question 4Textbook p. 249

      Answer

      In the surrounding water, the air-filled round flask tends to act as a diverging element because its inside has lower index. It can give a reduced upright view. Filling it with water greatly reduces the index contrast, so there is much less lens effect. Some distortion can remain from the glass wall.

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 251

      Answer

      Choose (b) d. The projected image is rotated 180° relative to the slide as seen from behind the projector. Rotating d by 180° gives p.

      Question 2Textbook p. 251

      Answer

      An overhead projector sends light upward through the transparency and lens. The projection head’s angled mirror turns the beam toward the screen and changes its orientation. With the transparency in the normal writing position, the viewer sees an upright image.

      Question 3Textbook p. 251

      Answer

      Place the target near the principal focus on the far side. Sunlight arrives nearly parallel, so it concentrates around the focal plane.

      Question 4Textbook p. 251

      Answer

      1. Put the spider 2f from the lens.
      2. Put the film or sensor 2f on the other side. Then |m| = dᵢ/dₒ = 1 and the image is real and inverted.
      Section review

      Question 1Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      Eyeglasses can use converging lenses for farsightedness or diverging lenses for nearsightedness. A cylindrical component can correct astigmatism.

      Question 2Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      1. For f = +50 cm, 1/dᵢ = 1/50 − 1/25 = −1/50 cm⁻¹. dᵢ = −50 cm, on the object side.
      2. It is virtual, upright, and twice as tall as the object.
      Question 3Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      At infinity the film is 50 mm from the lens, so f = 50 mm. With dₒ = 3000 mm, dᵢ = 1/(1/50 − 1/3000) ≈ 50.85 mm. Move the lens about 0.85 mm farther from the film.

      Question 4Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      Use dₒ = 400 mm and dᵢ = 20.0 mm. f = 1/(1/400 + 1/20.0) ≈ 19.0 mm.

      Question 5Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      dᵢ = 1/(1/20.0 − 1/80.0) = 26.67 cm. m = −26.67/80.0 = −⅓. The projected image is 1.7 cm tall and inverted.

      Question 6Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      dᵢ = 1/(1/20.0 − 1/30.0) = +60.0 cm. Signed m = −60.0/30.0 = −2.00. The image is real, inverted, and twice the object height.

      Question 7Textbook p. 252

      Answer

      Draw the straight ray from the object tip through the optical centre to the image tip. The two triangles with the principal axis are similar, so |hᵢ|/hₒ = |dᵢ|/dₒ. For an inverted real image, signed m = −dᵢ/dₒ.

      Question 8Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      1. 1/dᵢ = 1/(−6.0) − 1/10.0 = −1/3.75 cm⁻¹, giving dᵢ = −3.75 cm, about 3.8 cm from the lens.
      2. Virtual.
      3. Reduced.
      4. Upright.
      5. m = −(−3.75)/10.0 = 0.375. The image height is about 1.9 cm.
      6. On the same side as the object.
      Question 9Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      Flash light enters a dilated pupil, reflects from the back of the eye, and returns toward a camera close to the flash axis. Move the flash off axis, use more room light, or use a preflash to constrict the pupil.

      Question 10Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      Hypermetropia is farsightedness. With insufficient focusing power or an eye that is too short, rays from a nearby object would meet behind the retina. A converging corrective lens increases the incoming convergence.

      Question 11Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      Myopia is nearsightedness. With too much focusing power or a long eyeball, rays from a distant object meet in front of the retina. A diverging corrective lens moves the focus back onto the retina.

      Question 12Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      A conventional compound microscope rotates the view by 180°. The bug appears to move from the upper right to the lower left. The objective forms the inverted intermediate image, and the eyepiece magnifies it.

      Question 13Textbook p. 253

      Answer

      A Fresnel lens uses concentric stepped zones to reproduce the bending action of a much thicker curved lens. The reduced thickness and mass are useful for large apertures such as projector condensers.

      Question 1Textbook p. 254

      Answer

      A pinhole camera needs no lens or focus adjustment. A small hole can give a large depth of field. The trade-off is a dimmer image and possible blur from diffraction if the hole is too small.

      Question 2Textbook p. 254

      Answer

      William Herschel dispersed sunlight with a prism and compared thermometer readings across the spectrum. The thermometer just beyond the visible red end warmed, revealing radiation outside the visible range.

      Question 3Textbook p. 254

      Answer

      A streetlight viewed through fine mesh can show a starburst. The mesh openings and threads diffract the light into different directions.

      Question 6Textbook p. 254

      Question 1Textbook p. 258

      Answer

      Light refracts and disperses on entering a raindrop, reflects internally, and refracts and disperses again on exit.

      Question 2Textbook p. 258

      Answer

      Rayleigh scattering by air molecules preferentially redirects shorter visible wavelengths. Blue light scattered toward your eyes contributes strongly to the daytime sky colour.

      Question 3Textbook p. 258

      Answer

      At sunset, sunlight follows a long path through the atmosphere. Much of the blue light scatters out of the direct beam, leaving a greater proportion of red and orange light.

      Question 4Textbook p. 258

      Answer

      Refraction at the curved surfaces changes the direction of the rays and can bring them together or spread them apart.

      Question 5Textbook p. 258

      Answer

      Violet bends most in ordinary glass with normal dispersion. Red bends least.

      Answer

      Ultraviolet radiation causes tanning and sunburn.
